questions.passage: In the dry season, when taps in Ungwan Rimi ran only at midnight, Amina Bello worked in her father's bicycle workshop, turning old rims, a cut jerrycan and a brass float into a rain-collector. Her neighbours laughed at the funnel and the small bottle that rose to show when the tank was full. Undeterred, she fixed the device to the roof of the primary school. The first rain came at dusk, drumming on the zinc. By morning, the head teacher was filling buckets for the nursery class, and the neighbours who had laughed the week before were asking how the bottle worked. Amina wiped her hands on her wrapper and said nothing, but her eyes kept returning to the float, rising and falling, rising and falling, like the breathing of a patient who would live.
questions.q: The detail that the neighbours' laughter changes to questions mainly serves to
options: suggest that the head teacher is more popular than Amina.
show that their attitude has shifted from scorn to interest.
indicate that rain has stopped falling at the school.
prove that Amina enjoys mocking her neighbours.
questions.explanation: The same neighbours who laughed now ask how the bottle works, a shift from ridicule to curiosity. Nothing in the passage says the rain stopped or that Amina mocks them.

questions.q: A novelist lets the reader know that the letter in the servant's tray contains news that will ruin the household, while the master cheerfully takes it without suspicion. This technique is best described as
questions.explanation: The reader possesses information that the master lacks, so the master's cheerful ignorance creates dramatic irony. Verbal irony lies in what a speaker says, flashback returns to earlier events, and suspense is uncertainty about what will happen.

questions.q: A story is told by a narrator who is not a character in it and who enters the minds of different characters at will, revealing their private thoughts. The narrative technique used is
questions.explanation: A narrator outside the story with unrestricted access to several characters' minds is omniscient. First-person narration requires an 'I' narrator in the story, while limited third-person narration stays with one character's perspective.

questions.q: Identify the figure of speech in 'The new solar pump could lift a whole river before breakfast.'
questions.explanation: The claim that a pump could lift a whole river before breakfast is deliberate exaggeration for emphasis. There is no comparison using 'like' or 'as', and the statement is not an understatement or a substitute name for an associated idea.

questions.q: In 'The reservoir was a silver shield against the dry season,' the figure of speech used is
questions.explanation: The reservoir is directly called a shield, transferring the idea of protection without using 'like' or 'as', which makes it a metaphor. A simile would require an explicit comparison, metonymy would substitute an associated term, and litotes would use understatement through negation.

questions.q: An elder settles a quarrel by quoting a short, well-known saying that the parties must apply to their conduct. This oral form is a
questions.explanation: A proverb is a brief traditional saying that conveys community wisdom and is applied to a present situation. A riddle is a puzzle, an incantation is a verbal charm, and a dirge is a mourning song.

questions.q: A mother sings softly to a restless baby, repeating a simple tune until the child sleeps. Such an oral song is called a
questions.explanation: A lullaby is a soothing song sung to put a child to sleep. A dirge mourns the dead, a ballad narrates a story, and a panegyric is a formal poem of praise.

questions.q: A tale in which animals speak and act like people in order to teach a moral lesson is best classified as a
questions.explanation: A fable uses animal characters with human speech or behaviour to point to a moral lesson. An epic is a long heroic narrative, an elegy mourns the dead, and a panegyric praises a person.

questions.passage:
At dusk the maize fields bow their heads,
and Mother ties the last sheaf tight;
the pestle drums in the compound,
the yam barn swallows the light.
My father counts the sacks by twos,
then wipes his brow and hums a tune;
the children chase the scattered grain
beneath the rising harvest moon.
The fireflies stitch the dark with gold,
the tired earth breathes out and rests;
tomorrow's market waits with scales,
and hope sits warm in all our chests.
questions.q: In the poem, the phrase 'the yam barn swallows the light' mainly suggests that the barn
options: is so full of yams that it overflows with light
absorbs the fading daylight and becomes dark
has been abandoned because the harvest was poor
reflects the sunset with a golden glow
questions.explanation: At dusk the dark interior of the barn appears to take in or 'swallow' the remaining daylight, so the image conveys gathering darkness rather than brightness. The idea of a golden glow or light overflowing from stored yams treats the figure too literally and ignores the verb 'swallows'.

questions.passage:

and Mother ties the last sheaf tight;
the pestle drums in the compound,
the yam barn swallows the light.
My father counts the sacks by twos,

beneath the rising harvest moon.
The fireflies stitch the dark with gold,

tomorrow's market waits with scales,
and hope sits warm in all our chests.
questions.q: The contrast between the busy activities of the day and the restful evening chiefly helps to emphasise the
options: relief and hopeful expectation that follow honest labour
market's power to cheat the farmers
children's fear of the rising moon
father's regret over poor market sales
questions.explanation: The counting, tying and chasing belong to the work of harvest, while the evening brings rest, a warm earth and hope of tomorrow's market. This movement from toil to rest stresses satisfaction and expectation rather than fear, regret or cheating.

questions.q: A play that presents simplified characters in sensational situations and ends with virtue rewarded and vice punished is best described as
questions.explanation: Melodrama is marked by simplified moral types, sensational incidents and a clear victory of virtue over vice. Tragedy usually ends in disaster rather than moral reward, while farce aims at absurd physical comedy more than the rewarding of virtue.

questions.q: A group of villagers remains on stage throughout a play, speaks in unison and comments on the actions of the main characters. This technique is called
questions.explanation: When a group speaks together and comments on the main action, it functions as a chorus. A soliloquy is spoken by one character alone, an aside is a brief remark not meant for other characters, and a subplot is a secondary story.

questions.q: A pair of successive lines of verse, usually rhyming and sharing the same metre, is called
questions.explanation: A couplet consists of two successive lines, commonly rhyming and sharing a metre. A quatrain has four lines, a refrain is a repeated line or group of lines, and an octave has eight lines.

questions.q: A line of verse made up of six metrical feet is called
questions.explanation: Hexameter describes a line of six metrical feet, just as pentameter has five and tetrameter has four. Heptameter would have seven feet.

questions.passage: The generator coughed once, then settled into a worried rumble. Inside Mama Nkechi’s chemist, the bulbs flickered, and the fridge that kept the vaccines cold began to click like a tired insect. Chinedu counted the note in his palm: two hundred naira, enough for a litre of fuel but not for the bus home. He had promised his mother he would return before dark. Outside, the street was a river of shadows; traders were packing, and a boy was selling torch batteries with a voice already hoarse. Chinedu unscrewed the fuel cap, looked at the thin, bright line of fuel inside, and poured in only half. Then he hid the rest of the money under the plaster on his ankle and went back inside to apologise to the fridge.
questions.q: What does Chinedu’s decision to pour in only half of the fuel most strongly suggest about him?
options: He believes the generator will run better on half fuel.
He intends to sabotage the generator so that the shop closes.
He is afraid that the fuel will spill if the tank is filled.
He is balancing the need to keep the fridge running with the need to have money for his journey home.
questions.explanation: He has only enough money for a litre of fuel but also needs bus fare, so pouring half is a compromise between powering the fridge and keeping money for his return. The detail that he hides the rest of the money confirms that his concern is practical and financial, not a wish to damage the generator.

questions.passage: The generator coughed once, then settled into a worried rumble. Chinedu counted the note in his palm: two hundred naira, enough for a litre of fuel but not for the bus home. He had promised his mother he would return before dark. Chinedu unscrewed the fuel cap, looked at the thin, bright line of fuel inside, and poured in only half. Then he hid the rest of the money under the plaster on his ankle and went back inside to apologise to the fridge.
questions.q: The description of the fridge as beginning to click like a tired insect mainly conveys that
options: the refrigerator is struggling and close to failing as the power supply falters.
the chemist shop has been invaded by insects.
the fridge is new and unusually silent.
Chinedu is afraid of the machines in the shop.
questions.explanation: The simile makes the fridge sound weak and distressed, suggesting that the flickering power is threatening the vaccines. It does not literally introduce insects; the comparison is used to create an impression of strain.

questions.q: In a short story, a character’s room is described as having a neatly arranged desk, a faded family photograph turned face-down, and a shelf of unused medicine bottles. The writer offers no comment. This use of setting and objects mainly serves the narrative purpose of
options: indirectly revealing the occupant’s character and emotional state.
slowing the plot with an irrelevant digression.
questions.explanation: The careful arrangement, hidden photograph and unused bottles invite readers to infer orderliness, grief or unresolved illness without direct statement. This is indirect characterization through setting and possessions, not a frame story or mere digression.

questions.q: In a novel, Mama Eka tells her grandchildren a complete tale about a fisherman who rescued a river goddess, and after the tale the main action resumes in the compound. This technique of placing one story inside another is called
questions.explanation: A frame narrative encloses an inner tale within an outer setting or storytelling situation, as when the grandchildren’s listening frames the fisherman’s adventure. Interior monologue records thoughts, and dramatic irony depends on a gap between knowledge and events.

questions.q: Identify the figure of speech in the sentence 'Tunde said his new solar lamp could light up the whole of Lagos.'
questions.explanation: Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration for emphasis; saying a small solar lamp could light up an entire city is not meant literally. A simile would require a comparison using 'like' or 'as', and euphemism would soften a harsh idea.

questions.q: In the expression 'Pa Eze has gone to join the ancestors', the speaker is using
questions.explanation: The expression softly replaces the blunt statement that Pa Eze has died, which is the function of euphemism. It is not an exaggeration or a comparison introduced by 'like' or 'as'.

questions.q: Identify the figure of speech in the sentence 'The dry maize cobs crackled and popped in the fire as the fisherman warmed his hands.'
questions.explanation: The words 'crackled' and 'popped' imitate the sounds made by the cobs in the fire, which is onomatopoeia. The sentence does not give human qualities to the fire or use a direct comparison with 'like' or 'as'.

questions.q: In a storytelling session, the narrator often inserts a proverb at a moment of conflict. The chief effect of the proverb is to
options: summarise and comment on the situation while drawing out its lesson.
prove that the narrator can sing.
replace the need for a plot resolution.
questions.explanation: Proverbs in oral narrative commonly condense the meaning of an episode and direct the audience toward its moral or social lesson. They do not normally create a new setting or function as a substitute for resolving the story.

questions.q: The opening formula of many African folktales, such as 'Long ago, when the animals spoke like people', mainly serves to
options: announce that the performance is a riddle.
show that the story is a historical record with exact dates.
create a legendary, timeless setting for the tale.
questions.explanation: Such formulae signal that the audience is entering a story-world where ordinary rules may not apply. They do not claim exact historical dates or turn the folktale into a riddle.

questions.passage:
At first the letters sat like stones
on the page, and refused to move.
Then Ada traced one line alone,
and the stones became a drove
of goats that climbed a paper hill;
the library breathed in her ear:
'Go on, small reader, go until
the world you touch is clear.'
questions.q: The change from 'letters sat like stones' to the stones becoming 'a drove of goats' chiefly conveys that
options: Ada is beginning to make written words alive with meaning
the library has failed to provide a quiet place for study
Ada fears that farm animals have escaped into the library
Ada prefers stories about farming to other kinds of books
questions.explanation: The poem first compares letters to stubborn stones and then changes them into a moving herd, suggesting that Ada is beginning to make written words alive and meaningful. The goat image is not meant literally; it signals the imaginative transformation that reading brings.

questions.passage:
At first the letters sat like stones
on the page, and refused to move.
Then Ada traced one line alone,
and the stones became a drove
of goats that climbed a paper hill;
the library breathed in her ear:
'Go on, small reader, go until
the world you touch is clear.'
questions.q: The line 'the library breathed in her ear' is effective mainly because it
options: proves that the library is louder than a classroom
personifies the library as a gentle encourager of the young reader
shows that Ada is afraid of being watched by a ghost
suggests that the building is poorly ventilated
questions.explanation: The library is given the human action of breathing and speaking an encouragement into Ada's ear. This makes it a gentle presence urging her to keep reading rather than a mere building.

questions.passage:
At first the letters sat like stones
on the page, and refused to move.
Then Ada traced one line alone,
and the stones became a drove
of goats that climbed a paper hill;
the library breathed in her ear:
'Go on, small reader, go until
the world you touch is clear.'
questions.q: Which statement best expresses the main contrast in the poem?
options: The library changes its shape as Ada grows older
A page that first seems dead and stony becomes a living world through reading
A noisy library is preferred to a quiet farm
The reader finds arithmetic clearer than stories
questions.explanation: The opening shows the page as stony and resistant, while the later image and final lines show it opening into a clear world under the library's encouragement. The central movement is therefore from dead print to living meaning.

questions.q: A play staged in Makurdi in which characters such as Honesty, Greed and Death appear as persons is best classified as
questions.explanation: A morality play presents personified qualities or abstractions to teach a moral lesson, so characters like Honesty and Greed fit that form. A farce aims at exaggerated laughter, a chronicle play stages historical events, and a comedy of manners satirises social behaviour.

questions.q: The line 'O gentle moon, why do you hide your face?' illustrates the device known as
questions.explanation: Apostrophe is a direct address to an absent person, an object, or an abstract idea as if it could reply. The speaker's address to the moon therefore makes it apostrophe.

questions.q: The statement 'The more I learn, the less I know' is an example of
questions.explanation: A paradox is a statement that sounds self-contradictory but reveals a deeper truth, as the saying about learning does. Hyperbole exaggerates, euphemism softens, and onomatopoeia imitates sound.

questions.q: The quality of a narrative that makes its characters and events seem true to life is called
questions.explanation: Verisimilitude is the semblance of truth or lifelikeness in a narrative. Foreshadowing hints at later events, suspense creates anxious uncertainty, and satire ridicules through wit.

questions.passage: At midnight the rain came down as if the sky had been unstitched. By dawn, water had climbed the steps of St Mary's Primary School and was knocking politely at the doors of stalls near Ogbaru Main Market. Nnenna stood on the veranda with her youngest brother tied to her back, counting the jerrycans that bobbed past like noisy visitors. Across the road, Musa the tailor dragged his sewing machine onto a raft of planks while his neighbours passed sandbags from hand to hand, no one speaking the fear that hung above the roofs. When the first canoe arrived with dry garri and sachets of water, children ran to meet it, shouting as if it were a wedding. Only Mama Ebere remained seated on an upturned basin, fanning a small fire she had saved from the rain. 'If we weep every time the river visits,' she said, 'we will have no eyes left for the morning.'
questions.q: The expression 'as if the sky had been unstitched' mainly helps the reader to
options: see that the people were repairing the sky
understand that the rain was light and brief
picture the sky as a piece of torn cloth
feel the force and suddenness of the downpour
questions.explanation: The phrase compares the falling rain to a sky whose stitches have given way, conveying a sudden, overwhelming release. It is not meant literally, and it does not suggest a light or brief shower.

questions.passage: At midnight the rain came down as if the sky had been unstitched. By dawn, water had climbed the steps of St Mary's Primary School and was knocking politely at the doors of stalls near Ogbaru Main Market. Nnenna stood on the veranda with her youngest brother tied to her back, counting the jerrycans that bobbed past like noisy visitors. Across the road, Musa the tailor dragged his sewing machine onto a raft of planks while his neighbours passed sandbags from hand to hand, no one speaking the fear that hung above the roofs. When the first canoe arrived with dry garri and sachets of water, children ran to meet it, shouting as if it were a wedding. Only Mama Ebere remained seated on an upturned basin, fanning a small fire she had saved from the rain. 'If we weep every time the river visits,' she said, 'we will have no eyes left for the morning.'
questions.q: The detail about the jerrycans bobbing past 'like noisy visitors' chiefly contributes to the impression that
options: the flood has turned ordinary household objects into strange intruders
the flood was harmless and entertaining
Nnenna is too careless to notice danger
the market people are expecting a celebration
questions.explanation: The jerrycans are described as 'noisy visitors', making familiar containers seem like intruders moving through the flooded town. This deepens the sense of disruption; it does not show that the people are carefree or expecting a party.

questions.passage: At midnight the rain came down as if the sky had been unstitched. By dawn, water had climbed the steps of St Mary's Primary School and was knocking politely at the doors of stalls near Ogbaru Main Market. Nnenna stood on the veranda with her youngest brother tied to her back, counting the jerrycans that bobbed past like noisy visitors. Across the road, Musa the tailor dragged his sewing machine onto a raft of planks while his neighbours passed sandbags from hand to hand, no one speaking the fear that hung above the roofs. When the first canoe arrived with dry garri and sachets of water, children ran to meet it, shouting as if it were a wedding. Only Mama Ebere remained seated on an upturned basin, fanning a small fire she had saved from the rain. 'If we weep every time the river visits,' she said, 'we will have no eyes left for the morning.'
questions.q: Mama Ebere's statement at the end most strongly suggests that she
options: does not care about the suffering of her neighbours
meets the disaster with resilient humour and a forward-looking spirit
wants the people to stop preparing for the morning
believes the flood has ended for good
questions.explanation: Mama Ebere jokes that weeping at every flood would leave no eyes for the morning, which shows resilience and a focus on what comes next. She is not shown as uncaring or as denying the danger.

questions.q: A writer ends a chapter just as a character opens a door behind which a dangerous stranger is waiting, and the outcome is not revealed until the next chapter. This technique is best described as
questions.explanation: Suspense is created when the reader is kept waiting to learn the outcome of a tense situation. A flashback returns to earlier events, exposition supplies background, and denouement resolves the plot.

questions.q: Identify the figure of speech in the sentence: 'The rich trader had many servants but few friends; the poor farmer had many friends but few servants.'
questions.explanation: The sentence sets the rich trader's servants and friends against the poor farmer's friends and servants in a balanced contrast. This contrast is antithesis; there is no comparison using like or as, and no deliberate exaggeration.

questions.q: A short, memorable traditional saying that sums up a community's wisdom and is often quoted to support a moral point is called a
questions.explanation: A proverb is a brief traditional saying that carries communal wisdom and is quoted to support a point. A riddle tests wit, a dirge mourns the dead, and a praise name celebrates a person.

questions.passage:
Old Kano, at Dusk

From the north, slabs of salt come down
on camels patient as slow rain;
from southern groves, red kola crowns
the baskets borne along the plain.
At dusk the market opens its palms;
cowries whisper in traders' hands.
The north and south, in one warm wind,
price their long distance into coins.
questions.q: The simile in 'patient as slow rain' chiefly suggests that the camels are
options: bringing relief after a long drought
steady and unhurried in their movement
waiting for the rains to begin
questions.explanation: The comparison presents the camels as calm, slow and enduring as they carry salt. It does not say that they bring rain, make a sound, or are waiting for rain.

questions.passage:
Old Kano, at Dusk

From the north, slabs of salt come down
on camels patient as slow rain;
from southern groves, red kola crowns
the baskets borne along the plain.
At dusk the market opens its palms;
cowries whisper in traders' hands.
The north and south, in one warm wind,
price their long distance into coins.
questions.q: The phrase 'the market opens its palms' mainly presents the market as
options: angry at the traders from the north
secretive about the prices of goods
questions.explanation: The image of open palms suggests readiness to receive people and goods for trade. It conveys openness and exchange rather than emptiness, secrecy or anger.

questions.passage:
Old Kano, at Dusk

From the north, slabs of salt come down
on camels patient as slow rain;
from southern groves, red kola crowns
the baskets borne along the plain.
At dusk the market opens its palms;
cowries whisper in traders' hands.
The north and south, in one warm wind,
price their long distance into coins.
questions.q: The line 'price their long distance into coins' most nearly means that the market
options: prevents traders from moving between regions
turns the long journey between the regions into trade value
makes goods from far places cost nothing
questions.explanation: The phrase suggests that the distance travelled by goods becomes part of their worth when they are exchanged. It does not mean that distance is measured with coins or that movement is prevented.

questions.q: During a village meeting in Nsukka, the audience has already seen Uche replace the medicine in the chief's cup with poison, but the chief praises Uche and drinks it. The effect created is best described as
questions.explanation: Dramatic irony occurs when the audience knows more than a character on stage. The audience knows about the poison while the chief does not, which creates tension.

questions.q: A play about a family in Aba mixes a quarrel over rising market prices with the serious illness of their father. After much tension, the family reconciles and the sick man recovers. The play is best classified as
questions.explanation: A tragicomedy blends serious and comic elements, often moving towards reconciliation or recovery. A tragedy would end in disaster, and a farce would rely mainly on absurd physical humour.

questions.q: A line of verse containing four iambic feet is called
questions.explanation: An iambic foot has one unstressed syllable followed by a stressed syllable. Four such feet make iambic tetrameter; trimeter has three feet, while the other options name different kinds of feet.

questions.passage: At the Enugu State science fair, Ifeoma set up her water-filter project with two clear bottles, a bag of charcoal and a hand-lettered card reading 'Clean Water for Odo'. Her stall was modest, and she was proud of it. The judges moved from table to table, pausing at solar cookers and model bridges. Then Mrs Okafor, the chemistry teacher, stopped at the next stall and lifted a jar marked 'distilled water'. The liquid had a pale blue tint. 'Where did you get this?' she asked the boy behind the table. He smiled and said his uncle had supplied it from a laboratory in Onitsha. Ifeoma noticed the label on the lid: the same brand of bottled water sold in the school canteen. She looked away, but her hand began to shake. The bell rang for the next round. The boy's smile remained, and the judges moved on, one of them writing on his sheet with great care.
questions.q: From the passage, Ifeoma's shaking hand most strongly suggests that she
options: has recognised that the blue liquid may be ordinary bottled water presented as distilled water
is uncertain about the source of the charcoal in her filter
is angry that the judges have not yet visited her stall
is afraid that her own filter will be disqualified by Mrs Okafor
questions.explanation: Ifeoma has just connected the label on the jar's lid with the bottled water sold in the school canteen and then looks away, so her reaction points to suspicion of deception. The other descriptions misread her reaction as concern about her own project, the judges' movement, or her filter materials.

questions.passage: At the Enugu State science fair, Ifeoma set up her water-filter project with two clear bottles, a bag of charcoal and a hand-lettered card reading 'Clean Water for Odo'. Her stall was modest, and she was proud of it. The judges moved from table to table, pausing at solar cookers and model bridges. Then Mrs Okafor, the chemistry teacher, stopped at the next stall and lifted a jar marked 'distilled water'. The liquid had a pale blue tint. 'Where did you get this?' she asked the boy behind the table. He smiled and said his uncle had supplied it from a laboratory in Onitsha. Ifeoma noticed the label on the lid: the same brand of bottled water sold in the school canteen. She looked away, but her hand began to shake. The bell rang for the next round. The boy's smile remained, and the judges moved on, one of them writing on his sheet with great care.
questions.q: The final sentence of the passage mainly creates a mood of
options: cheerful triumph at the success of the fair
warm admiration for the judges' careful work
uneasy uncertainty about whether the deception will be noticed
calm relief that the bell has ended the round
questions.explanation: The boy's smile remains while a judge writes with care, leaving unresolved whether the suspicious entry will be exposed. This produces suspense and unease rather than celebration, admiration, or relief.

questions.q: A novel opens at Chief Uduak's funeral and then returns to the events of the week before his death to explain how the family reached that point. This structural arrangement is best described as
questions.explanation: The narrative moves back in time after the funeral to recount earlier events, which is the essence of a flashback. Foreshadowing only hints at later events, while suspense creates uncertainty about what will happen next.

questions.q: The narrator of a novel interrupts the story to say, 'Let the reader judge whether Adaeze acted wisely.' This technique is an example of
questions.explanation: The narrator steps out of the action to address readers directly and invite their judgement, a clear case of authorial intrusion. Interior monologue presents a character's inner thoughts, while dramatic irony depends on readers knowing more than the characters do.

questions.q: A novel presents the main events of a science fair inside an old teacher's account to her grandchildren, and the novel returns to the grandchildren at the end. This structure is best described as
questions.explanation: The grandchildren's outside situation encloses the teacher's inner story, so it functions as a frame narrative. A subplot is a secondary line of action, and an epistolary narrative is told through letters or similar documents.

questions.q: Identify the figure of speech in the sentence: 'The sun smiled on the science fair.'
questions.explanation: Smiling is a human action given to the sun, which makes the sentence an example of personification. A simile would use 'like' or 'as', while an apostrophe addresses an absent person or thing.

questions.q: 'I have a house with no door; what am I?' A short traditional puzzle of this kind, used to test wit, is called a
questions.explanation: A riddle is a brief oral puzzle whose answer tests the listener's wit or knowledge. A proverb is a wise saying, while an incantation is a spoken charm or magical formula.

questions.passage:
The Final Whistle

We lost the cup in Kaduna on Sunday afternoon,
the crowd went home with voices turned to rust.
Our captain stood alone beside the moon
and watched our colours settle into dust.

He did not curse the referee or rain,
nor blame the ball that struck the iron post.
He gathered us like seedlings after pain
and taught us how to lose before we boast.

Now in the locker, on the wooden shelf,
the empty space has memorised our name.
We wear our failure like a second self
and practise passing till the morning came.
questions.q: The phrase 'voices turned to rust' mainly suggests that the supporters' voices had become
options: completely silent in respect for the players
questions.explanation: Rust suggests decay and loss of brightness, so the voices have become worn, hoarse and dulled after the defeat. The phrase does not mean that the crowd became cheerful, nor does it mean that the supporters were completely silent.
